free_tier.stated: Open protocols: TCP / UDP / HTTP / HTTPS; open ports: 10000 to 60000; auth token: public.freefrp.com. [translated]

egress.terms: No byte quota is published. The page warns that sustained bandwidth at or above 30 Mbps will get the /24 banned.; ingress: udp

interface_detail: Standard frpc against a published server and token.
chaining: A no-identity UDP entry point that can front a WG listener, at the cost of an address that may move.
binding_note: No byte cap exists, so the 30 Mbps sustained threshold is the first thing that fails: it is a rate, and 1 TiB/month needs only 3.24 Mbps, so the quota test can pass while a burst still gets the address banned.

identity_cost.detail: No account: the page publishes the server address, port, version and a shared auth token.

reliability_note: The operator warns the IP may change at any time and that sustained 30 Mbps gets the whole /24 blocked.
confidence_note: The endpoint, port range, protocols and ban threshold are all on the page today.

evidence.proved: TCP/UDP/HTTP/HTTPS on ports 10000-60000, shared token, 30 Mbps sustained triggers a ban, IP may change without notice

notes: The most permissive free endpoint in the sweep: no account, no quota, UDP in the port range. Unlimited here means the operator publishes no byte cap, not that it promises unmetered capacity. It is a single volunteer server with an explicit no-SLA warning, so the binding is reliability, not volume. The /24 ban means a shared address takes neighbours with it.

extras.wg_detail: A raw frps endpoint with a shared token and a 10000-60000 port range; a WG datagram can be proxied on any port in that range, subject to frp's UDP session handling.
extras.volume_stated: No byte quota is published. The page warns that sustained bandwidth at or above 30 Mbps will get the /24 banned.
extras.transit_note: One volunteer server carries the datagrams.
